MERCHANT FEED CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Will this product feed get items disapproved?

Paste, load, or drop a Google Merchant Center or Meta Catalog product feed and get a deterministic, item-by-item report against the published product-data specification: missing required fields, invalid GTIN/MPN identifiers, malformed prices, and known promotional-text disapproval triggers.

Nothing is uploaded. The file you load is read in this browser and never leaves your device.

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a CI gate before you sync the feed?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file — run it right before your feed generator uploads to Merchant Center or Commerce Manager, or on a schedule against the file your CMS/Shopify/WooCommerce export produces:

node cli.mjs check feed.csv                    # human-readable, exit 1 if any error is found
node cli.mjs check feed.csv --json
node cli.mjs check feed.csv --max-warnings 0   # also fail the build on warnings

Get cli.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install. It reads only the local file you name: no network call, ever.

What this checks — and what it cannot

Documented disapproval reasonChecked here as

Sources and the exact spec limits used: why products get disapproved in Google Merchant Center, and what a feed checker can and can't see. Also worth a pass: Structured Data Drift Check, which catches your product pages' own JSON-LD drifting from what Google's Merchant Center feed rules expect it to match. Building or routing feeds to many channels day to day? See this checker vs. DataFeedWatch. Wondering whether scanning the feed yourself is enough? See this checker vs. eyeballing the feed in a spreadsheet.

Common questions

Does this guarantee my products will be approved?

No. It checks feed data-specification conformance — required fields, formats, GTIN checksums, enum values — which is one documented category of disapproval reason. It cannot see your Merchant Center or Commerce Manager account, your website's trust signals, or Shopping policy review, so it cannot detect misrepresentation, prohibited-product, or landing-page-mismatch disapprovals. Read the full scope on the docs page before relying on a clean report.

Is my product feed uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser page parses a pasted or locally loaded file entirely in your own browser and never sends it anywhere. The CLI reads only a local file — no network call, ever.

What feed formats does it accept?

CSV or TSV with a header row (Google's text feed format, or an export from Shopify, WooCommerce, or BigCommerce), or a JSON array of item objects (or {items:[...]}), the shape Meta's Catalog API and many feed tools already use. Column names are matched by common aliases (id/sku/item_id, image_link/image_url, and so on).

How is the GTIN checked?

With the real GS1 check-digit algorithm used for UPC-A, EAN-13, and GTIN-8/12/14 — the same arithmetic barcode scanners use to reject a mistyped code. A GTIN that is the right length but fails the checksum is very likely a typo, not a real product identifier.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not advice about Shopping Ads policy, account-level compliance, or whether Google or Meta will approve any specific listing — it reports whether the feed data you supplied conforms to the published product-data specification, nothing more. It does not fetch your landing pages and cannot confirm price, availability, or content there matches your feed. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use, including a disapproved listing, a suspended account, or lost ad spend.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. The feed you load is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded, file_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Only the barcode column in doubt? The GTIN List Check validates check digits and restores zeros Excel dropped, for any product list. It runs in your browser and the file is never uploaded.

Running Google Ads too? Drop your search terms report into the Google Ads wasted spend analyzer to see how much went to searches that never converted and which negative keywords are safe to add. It runs in your browser and the file is never uploaded.

Free and open source. If this saved you some digging, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

Merchant Feed Check vs. DataFeedWatch

Two different shapes: DataFeedWatch connects to your store, transforms your product feed with rules you build, and exports it to many advertising channels — an ongoing subscription account. This page is a free, no-account checker for one question — does a feed you already have conform to Google Merchant Center's and Meta Catalog's own published product-data specification — before it syncs.

What each tool is for

DataFeedWatch is product-feed management software, sold under an ongoing subscription account to e-commerce sellers and agencies. It connects to your store or feed source, lets you build transformation rules — title templates, category mapping, attribute enrichment, custom labels — and exports the optimized result to many advertising and marketplace channels. Setting it up means creating an account, connecting a data source, and configuring channel-specific export templates, not a one-off check. DataFeedWatch's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific plan names, product-count tiers, or pricing, so only its well-documented category and identity are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page.

This checker does none of that. It does not connect to a store, build transformation rules, or export a feed anywhere. It takes a feed you already have — CSV, TSV, or JSON, pasted or loaded from a file — and reports, item by item, exactly what would fail Google Merchant Center's or Meta Catalog's own published product-data specification: missing required fields, invalid GTIN/MPN checksums, malformed prices and availability values, and known promotional-text disapproval triggers. It runs free in any browser, and the same logic ships as a zero-dependency Node CLI you can run as a CI gate right before your feed generator syncs. No account, no upload, nothing stored.

QuestionWhere to answer it

I want to know whether the feed I already have would get items disapproved, before I sync it.This checker — free, instant, no account, nothing uploaded.
I want the same check to run automatically before every deploy, as a CI gate.This checker's zero-dependency CLI (cli.mjs), run against the file your generator produces.
I need channel-specific field mapping, category rules, and multi-channel export.DataFeedWatch, or a comparable platform — this checker has none of those features.
Why do products actually get disapproved, beyond a failed check?This checker's disapproval-reasons page.
Do I need an account or a connected data source to use the tool?This checker: no. DataFeedWatch and comparable platforms are sold through an ongoing account.

A seller running feeds to several channels gets different value from each: DataFeedWatch (or a comparable platform) for building and routing an optimized feed day to day under an ongoing subscription, and a free checker like this one for an instant, no-login answer to whether a feed conforms to the published spec, wired into CI if you want it there. This page's own report is a deterministic read of the feed you loaded, not a guarantee that Google or Meta will approve any specific listing.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: the browser page parses a pasted or locally loaded file entirely in your own browser, and the CLI reads only a local file. Neither ever sends your feed anywhere.

Should I use this checker or DataFeedWatch?

They do different jobs, and a seller running feeds to several channels will likely end up touching both. Setting it up means an account, connecting a data source, and configuring channel-specific export templates, not a one-off check. It takes a feed you already have -- CSV, TSV, or JSON -- and reports exactly which items would be flagged against Google Merchant Center's and Meta Catalog's own published product-data specification: missing required fields, invalid GTIN/MPN checksums, malformed prices, and known promotional-text disapproval triggers. vs-eyeballing-the-feed-in-a-spreadsheet..text:
← Merchant Feed Check

Merchant Feed Check vs. eyeballing the feed in a spreadsheet

Opening the feed in a spreadsheet and scanning it row by row is the normal first check before a sync, and it works well for the obvious case — a screaming promotional title, a repeated SKU. Two of the most common documented disapproval reasons are specifically the kind that look like ordinary data on a visual scan, because the value that fails is the same length and shape as every valid value around it.

A four-row feed, checked both ways

Take a feed with one clean row and three rows each carrying a different problem. This is the exact feed this page's own test runs through checkFeed() — nothing below is invented.

RowWhat a spreadsheet scan seesWhat checkFeed() reports
sku-1A normal-looking row: real title, real description, a 13-digit GTIN, a priced-and-in-stock item.0 errors, 0 warnings — correctly passes.
sku-2Looks wrong immediately: GREAT DEAL Red Hoodie 50% off Free Shipping, a 5-character description, not-a-url for the link, maybe for availability, cheap for a price.5 errors, 4 warnings — the checker catches the same row a careful reviewer already flags on sight.
sku-3Looks identical to sku-1. Same title shape, same description length, a 13-digit all-numeric GTIN sitting in the same column as every other valid one.Exactly 1 error: invalid-gtin-checksum. The GTIN is 4006381339931 against sku-1's 4006381333931 — two digits transposed, same length, same shape, fails the GS1 check-digit calculation.
sku-4Looks identical to sku-1. Price column reads 19.99, which is what every price in the sheet looks like once the spreadsheet software applies its own currency formatting.Exactly 1 error: invalid-price-format. The underlying value is 19.99 with no currency code, and the required shape is NUMBER CURRENCY, e.g. 19.99 USD.

Feed-level total, from the same test: 4 items, 3 with at least one error, 7 errors and 4 warnings overall. Two of those three flagged rows (sku-3 and sku-4) would not draw a second look in a spreadsheet — nothing about them differs visually from the row directly above.

Why the checksum and the format rule are the quiet ones

A GTIN is 8, 12, 13, or 14 digits. A single mistyped or transposed digit produces another number of the exact same length, made entirely of digits — it does not look different from a valid one in the next cell. Telling them apart means running the GS1 check-digit calculation on every row: weight each digit of the payload 3 and 1 alternating from the digit immediately left of the check digit, sum the weighted digits, and the check digit must equal (10 - sum mod 10) mod 10. That is not a check anyone runs by hand across a feed of any real size.

The price format rule is quieter still, because the failure is an absence rather than a wrong value. Google's and Meta's shared spec requires NUMBER CURRENCY — 19.99 USD, not 19.99 or $19.99. A spreadsheet applying its own currency number format renders 19.99, $19.99, and 19.99 USD as visually similar cells; nothing on screen signals that the underlying string never carried the required three-letter code.

Common questions

Why doesn't scanning the feed by eye catch a bad GTIN?

A GTIN is a 13-digit (or 8/12/14-digit) number, and a transposed or mistyped digit produces another number of the exact same length made entirely of digits -- it looks identical to a valid one sitting in the next cell. Telling the two apart means running the GS1 check-digit calculation (weight each digit 3/1 alternating from the right, sum, and the check digit must equal (10 - sum mod 10) mod 10), which nobody does by eye on a 2,000-row feed. Google and Meta both run this calculation and reject the mismatch as a bad or missing product identifier.

Why doesn't scanning the feed by eye catch a missing currency code?

The published price format is "NUMBER CURRENCY", e.g. "19.99 USD" -- but a bare "19.99" reads as a completely ordinary price to anyone scanning the column, especially in a spreadsheet where every other price cell is formatted as currency by the spreadsheet software itself, hiding that the underlying feed value never carries the required currency code. The rejection only shows up once the feed is parsed against the spec's exact regular-expression shape, not from looking at the rendered column.

What does a spreadsheet scan catch that this checker doesn't add much to?

A title in all caps with "50% OFF" and "FREE SHIPPING" in it, or the same SKU appearing on two rows, both look wrong on sight -- this checker flags the same two rows for the same reasons, so a careful reviewer scanning for those specific shapes was already going to catch them. The value here is narrow: two specific, well-documented rejection reasons that are constructed to look like ordinary data on a visual scan, checked mechanically on every row instead of on however many rows get a close look.

Does this replace reviewing the feed before it syncs?

No. It is a deterministic, row-by-row check against Google's and Meta's own published product-data specification, not a review of whether the products, pricing, or category placement make business sense. A reviewer scanning the feed still catches the obviously wrong-looking rows and anything domain-specific this tool has no rule for; this checker adds the two specific, quiet failure modes a visual scan is structurally unlikely to catch.

Nothing here says a spreadsheet review is a bad first check — it is exactly right for the case it is good at. This page describes two specific, narrow failure modes that are constructed to look like ordinary data, not a fault in reviewers.

Check your own feed

Paste or load your feed — CSV, TSV, or JSON — and get the same per-row report, including the GTIN checksum and price-format checks a visual scan cannot run.

Open Merchant Feed Check

Also worth a pass if you route the same feed to many channels: this checker vs. DataFeedWatch.

why-products-get-disapproved-in-google-m.text:
← Back to Merchant Feed Check

Why products get disapproved in Google Merchant Center — and what a feed checker can't see

Google Merchant Center and Meta Commerce Manager both reject individual product-feed items for reasons that fall into two very different categories, and conflating them is how a merchant ends up trusting a tool that cannot actually tell them what they need to know.

Category 1: data-specification problems — checkable from the feed alone

These are objective, deterministic checks against the published product-data specification. A feed file either conforms or it doesn't, with no need to know anything about the merchant's account, website, or business.

ReasonWhy it's common
Missing unique product identifier (GTIN/MPN + brand)Most product categories require it; sellers of handmade, refurbished, or private-label goods often have neither a real GTIN nor a way to get one, and skip the explicit identifier_exists: false opt-out that would make the omission valid.
Malformed price or availability fieldA bare number without a currency code, a currency symbol instead of an ISO code, or a free-text availability value ("Ships in 3 days" instead of in stock) is a common export-tool mistake.
Promotional or price text in the title or descriptionCopy written for a storefront ("50% off today only!") is reused verbatim in the feed without editing it for Shopping's stricter title/description rules.
Missing required attributeA CMS export that drops a field for any item missing a value (many plugins omit empty columns entirely) silently produces an incomplete row.
Duplicate item IDsA feed regenerated from two overlapping data sources, or a variant-handling bug, produces the same ID twice — the platform typically keeps only one and silently drops the other.

Merchant Feed Check checks every row in this table deterministically — see its own report for exactly which rule fired and why.

Category 2: account and policy problems — invisible to any feed checker

These require Google's or Meta's own crawl of the merchant's actual website, or a human policy reviewer, and no tool that only reads a feed file can evaluate them:

  • Misrepresentation / insufficient trust signals — missing business verification, no visible contact information, thin or templated site content. This is an assessment of the whole website, not the feed.
  • Prohibited or restricted products — category-specific policy, decided against the product itself, not its feed formatting.
  • Landing page mismatch — the feed's price or availability must match what a shopper actually sees on the linked page at crawl time. A feed checker can confirm the format is valid; it cannot fetch and compare the live page.
  • Account-level suspension — a policy violation found anywhere in the account, applied to the whole feed regardless of any individual item's quality.

If a feed passes every check here and items are still disapproved, the cause is almost always in this second category — read the specific disapproval reason Merchant Center or Commerce Manager gives in your dashboard, since that is the only place these are visible.

Wiring the CLI into a deploy pipeline

Run it as a step right before whatever job uploads or syncs your feed — a scheduled GitHub Action, a cron job, or a step in the same pipeline that regenerates the feed from your product database:

- name: Check product feed
  run: node cli.mjs check feed.csv

Exit code 1 fails the job on any data-specification error, so a broken feed never reaches the sync step. Ecosystem note: this reads the feed file itself, so it works the same whether that file came from Shopify's native feed app, a WooCommerce plugin export, or a hand-rolled script — nothing here depends on which platform generated it.

Common questions

What is the single most common Merchant Center disapproval reason?

Missing or invalid unique product identifiers — a missing GTIN, MPN, or brand where the product category requires one — is consistently named as the most common data-quality disapproval across Google's own Merchant Center help content and seller community threads. A feed checker can verify the identifier is present and, for GTIN, that the check digit is mathematically valid; it cannot verify the GTIN is the correct one for that specific product.

Can a feed checker guarantee my products will be approved?

No. Disapprovals fall into two categories: data-specification problems, which a feed checker can catch, and account/policy problems — misrepresentation, prohibited products, insufficient trust signals, a landing page that does not match the feed — which require Google's or Meta's own crawl and account review and are invisible to a tool that only reads a feed file.

Why doesn't Dependabot-style automation exist for this already?

Google and Meta each publish a free, web-form feed validator, but neither ships a scriptable, zero-account CLI a merchant can wire into their own deploy pipeline the way a linter runs in CI, so a broken feed is caught only when a human remembers to paste it into a web form, or after the crawler already rejected it.

No warranty. This page is informational commentary on publicly documented Merchant Center and Commerce Manager policy categories, not legal or compliance advice, and not a guarantee of approval outcomes. Policies change; verify current requirements against Google's and Meta's own published help documentation before relying on anything here.

Also see Structured Data Drift Check, which catches a product page's own JSON-LD drifting from its visible copy — a different input Google's Shopping features can also read.

Support this project — optional, never required.
